claim: Extant ecdysozoans are represented by a great variety of soft-bodied or articulated organisms that may or may not have appendages.
source: Extant ecdysozoans (moulting animals) are represented by a great variety of soft-bodied or articulated organisms that may or may not have appendages.
evidence: This is a statement about the diversity of extant ecdysozoans based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Controversies remain about the vermiform nature of the ancestral ecdysozoan body plan.
source: However, controversies remain about the vermiform nature (i.e. elongated and tubular) of their ancestral body plan.
evidence: This statement acknowledges ongoing scientific debate without providing specific supporting evidence.

claim: Beretella spinosa is a tiny ecdysozoan with a maximal length of 3 mm.
source: We describe here Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov. a tiny (maximal length 3 mm) ecdysozoan from the lowermost Cambrian, Yanjiahe Formation, South China, characterized by an unusual sack-like appearance, single opening, and spiny ornament.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported from the fossil specimens described in the study.

claim: Beretella spinosa is from the lowermost Cambrian Yanjiahe Formation in South China.
source: We describe here Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov. a tiny (maximal length 3 mm) ecdysozoan from the lowermost Cambrian, Yanjiahe Formation, South China, characterized by an unusual sack-like appearance, single opening, and spiny ornament.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the geological provenance of the fossil specimens.

claim: Beretella spinosa is characterized by an unusual sack-like appearance, single opening, and spiny ornament.
source: We describe here Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov. a tiny (maximal length 3 mm) ecdysozoan from the lowermost Cambrian, Yanjiahe Formation, South China, characterized by an unusual sack-like appearance, single opening, and spiny ornament.
evidence: These are morphological observations made directly from the fossil specimens.

claim: Beretella spinosa has no equivalent among animals except Saccorhytus coronarius.
source: Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov has no equivalent among animals, except Saccorhytus coronarius, also from the basal Cambrian.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on morphological analysis of known animal taxa.

claim: Saccorhytus coronarius is from the basal Cambrian.
source: Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov has no equivalent among animals, except Saccorhytus coronarius, also from the basal Cambrian.
evidence: This is a statement about the geological age of Saccorhytus coronarius.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses resolve Beretella and Saccorhytus as a sister group (Saccorhytida) to all known Ecdysozoa.
source: Phylogenetic analyses resolve both fossil species as a sister group (Saccorhytida) to all known Ecdysozoa, thus suggesting that ancestral ecdysozoans may have been non-vermiform animals.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analyses performed in the study.

claim: Ancestral ecdysozoans may have been non-vermiform animals.
source: Phylogenetic analyses resolve both fossil species as a sister group (Saccorhytida) to all known Ecdysozoa, thus suggesting that ancestral ecdysozoans may have been non-vermiform animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic position of Saccorhytida.

claim: Saccorhytids are likely to represent an early off-shot along the stem-line Ecdysozoa.
source: Saccorhytids are likely to represent an early off-shot along the stem-line Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the phylogenetic position of Saccorhytida.

claim: The Saccorhytida lineage became extinct during the Cambrian.
source: Although it became extinct during the Cambrian, this animal lineage provides precious insight into the early evolution of Ecdysozoa and the nature of the earliest representatives of the group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of saccorhytids in post-Cambrian fossil records.

claim: The Saccorhytida lineage provides insight into the early evolution of Ecdysozoa.
source: Although it became extinct during the Cambrian, this animal lineage provides precious insight into the early evolution of Ecdysozoa and the nature of the earliest representatives of the group.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: The Ediacaran-Cambrian transition is marked by the appearance of a variety of new body plans in the fossil record.
source: The Ediacaran‒Cambrian transition is marked by the appearance in the fossil record of a variety of new body plans that prefigure the majority of present-day animal lineages, including the ecdysozoans, a huge clade that encompasses all invertebrate animals growing through successive moulting stages, such as panarthropods (Arthropoda, Onychophora, Tardigrada), scalidophoran (incl. Priapulida) and nematoid worms (Erwin, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Erwin, 2020.

claim: Ecdysozoans encompass all invertebrate animals growing through successive moulting stages.
source: The Ediacaran‒Cambrian transition is marked by the appearance in the fossil record of a variety of new body plans that prefigure the majority of present-day animal lineages, including the ecdysozoans, a huge clade that encompasses all invertebrate animals growing through successive moulting stages, such as panarthropods (Arthropoda, Onychophora, Tardigrada), scalidophoran (incl. Priapulida) and nematoid worms (Erwin, 2020).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about ecdysozoans supported by citation.

claim: Ecdysozoans include panarthropods, scalidophoran, and nematoid worms.
source: The Ediacaran‒Cambrian transition is marked by the appearance in the fossil record of a variety of new body plans that prefigure the majority of present-day animal lineages, including the ecdysozoans, a huge clade that encompasses all invertebrate animals growing through successive moulting stages, such as panarthropods (Arthropoda, Onychophora, Tardigrada), scalidophoran (incl. Priapulida) and nematoid worms (Erwin, 2020).
evidence: This is a taxonomic statement supported by citation.

claim: Ecdysozoans represent a very high percentage of animal biodiversity and disparity.
source: Altogether ecdysozoans represent a very high percentage of animal biodiversity and disparity, inhabiting almost all possible ecological niches on Earth (Brusca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brusca et al., 2016.

claim: Ecdysozoans inhabit almost all possible ecological niches on Earth.
source: Altogether ecdysozoans represent a very high percentage of animal biodiversity and disparity, inhabiting almost all possible ecological niches on Earth (Brusca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brusca et al., 2016.

claim: The nature of the last common ancestor of Ecdysozoa remains largely unresolved.
source: The nature of the last common ancestor of Ecdysozoa (LCAE) remains largely unresolved, even though worms are prevalent before the rise of panarthropods as trace and body fossils in basal Cambrian and late Ediacaran rocks (Buatois et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Worms are prevalent before the rise of panarthropods as trace and body fossils in basal Cambrian and late Ediacaran rocks.
source: The nature of the last common ancestor of Ecdysozoa (LCAE) remains largely unresolved, even though worms are prevalent before the rise of panarthropods as trace and body fossils in basal Cambrian and late Ediacaran rocks (Buatois et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fossil evidence.

claim: Some recent molecular phylogenies predict that the most basal ecdysozoans were worm-like, elongated organisms.
source: Some recent molecular phylogenies also predict that the most basal ecdysozoans were worm-like, elongated organisms (Howard et al., 2022; Laumer et al., 2019) that possibly diverged in the Ediacaran (Howard et al., 2022; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Basal ecdysozoans possibly diverged in the Ediacaran.
source: Some recent molecular phylogenies also predict that the most basal ecdysozoans were worm-like, elongated organisms (Howard et al., 2022; Laumer et al., 2019) that possibly diverged in the Ediacaran (Howard et al., 2022; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Current reconstruction based on fossil and developmental evidence features the ancestral ecdysozoan as a millimeter-sized worm.
source: Current reconstruction based on fossil and developmental evidence features the ancestral ecdysozoan as a millimeter-sized worm (Budd, 2001; Valentine and Collins, 2000) with a terminal (Ortega-Hernández et al., 2019) or ventral mouth (Martín-Durán and Hejnol, 2015; Nielsen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fossil and developmental studies.

claim: The ancestral ecdysozoan had a terminal or ventral mouth.
source: Current reconstruction based on fossil and developmental evidence features the ancestral ecdysozoan as a millimeter-sized worm (Budd, 2001; Valentine and Collins, 2000) with a terminal (Ortega-Hernández et al., 2019) or ventral mouth (Martín-Durán and Hejnol, 2015; Nielsen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mouth position.

claim: Saccorhytus was discovered in the basal Cambrian of China (Kuanchuanpu Formation; ca. 535 Ma).
source: Clearly, the discovery of Saccorhytus (Han et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020) in the basal Cambrian of China (Kuanchuanpu Formation; ca. 535 Ma Sawaki et al., 2008) that is anything but a worm sowed doubt among scientists.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery and geological dating.

claim: Saccorhytus is a sac-like secondarily phosphatized microscopic animal spiked with conical sclerites and a single opening.
source: Saccorhytus is a sac-like secondarily phosphatized microscopic animal spiked with conical sclerites and a single opening that was first seen as the earliest known deuterostome (Han et al., 2017) but is now considered as an ecdysozoan on more solid grounds (Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020), thus broadening the anatomical spectrum of the group and its disparity in the Cambrian and reopening the debate on the nature of LCAE.
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by citations.

claim: Saccorhytus was first seen as the earliest known deuterostome.
source: Saccorhytus is a sac-like secondarily phosphatized microscopic animal spiked with conical sclerites and a single opening that was first seen as the earliest known deuterostome (Han et al., 2017) but is now considered as an ecdysozoan on more solid grounds (Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020), thus broadening the anatomical spectrum of the group and its disparity in the Cambrian and reopening the debate on the nature of LCAE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original interpretation.

claim: Saccorhytus is now considered as an ecdysozoan.
source: Saccorhytus is a sac-like secondarily phosphatized microscopic animal spiked with conical sclerites and a single opening that was first seen as the earliest known deuterostome (Han et al., 2017) but is now considered as an ecdysozoan on more solid grounds (Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020), thus broadening the anatomical spectrum of the group and its disparity in the Cambrian and reopening the debate on the nature of LCAE.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reinterpretations.

claim: Beretella spinosa is from Member 5 of the Yanjiahe Formation (basal Cambrian Stage 2, ca. 529 Ma, Hubei Province, China).
source: We describe here Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov. from Member 5 of the Yanjiahe Formation (basal Cambrian Stage 2, ca. 529 Ma, Hubei Province, China) that shares morphological traits with Saccorhytus coronarius such as an ellipsoidal body, a pronounced bilaterality, a spiny ornament made of broad-based sclerites, and a single opening.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the geological provenance and age of the fossil.

claim: Beretella spinosa shares morphological traits with Saccorhytus coronarius including an ellipsoidal body, pronounced bilaterality, spiny ornament made of broad-based sclerites, and a single opening.
source: We describe here Beretella spinosa gen. et sp. nov. from Member 5 of the Yanjiahe Formation (basal Cambrian Stage 2, ca. 529 Ma, Hubei Province, China) that shares morphological traits with Saccorhytus coronarius such as an ellipsoidal body, a pronounced bilaterality, a spiny ornament made of broad-based sclerites, and a single opening.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: Saccorhytida first appeared in the literature as a new stem-group Deuterostomia that accommodated a single species, Saccorhytus coronarius.
source: Saccorhytida first appeared in the literature as a new stem-group Deuterostomia that accommodated a single species, Saccorhytus coronarius (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original publication.

claim: Saccorhytus is no longer considered a primitive deuterostome and more likely belongs to ecdysozoans.
source: Since Saccorhytus is no longer considered a primitive deuterostome and, instead, more likely belongs to ecdysozoans, Saccorhytida became an extinct Order of Ecdysozoa (Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reinterpretations.

claim: Saccorhytida became an extinct Order of Ecdysozoa.
source: Since Saccorhytus is no longer considered a primitive deuterostome and, instead, more likely belongs to ecdysozoans, Saccorhytida became an extinct Order of Ecdysozoa (Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020).
evidence: This is a taxonomic statement supported by citations.

claim: Saccorhytida is tentatively elevated to the rank of phylum within Ecdysozoa.
source: Because both Saccorhytus and Beretella display major morphological differences with all other known ecdysozoan phyla (Nematoida, Scalidophora, and Panarthropoda), Saccorhytida is tentatively elevated here to the rank of phylum within Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is a taxonomic decision based on morphological differences.

claim: Saccorhytus and Beretella display major morphological differences with all other known ecdysozoan phyla (Nematoida, Scalidophora, and Panarthropoda).
source: Because both Saccorhytus and Beretella display major morphological differences with all other known ecdysozoan phyla (Nematoida, Scalidophora, and Panarthropoda), Saccorhytida is tentatively elevated here to the rank of phylum within Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: Saccorhytida has a microscopic, ellipsoidal body shape with pronounced bilateral symmetry expressed by paired spiny sclerites.
source: Microscopic, ellipsoidal body shape with pronounced bilateral symmetry expressed by paired spiny sclerites.
evidence: This is part of the emended diagnosis based on morphological observations.

claim: Saccorhytida has a single, presumably oral opening on assumed ventral side with no anus.
source: Single, presumably oral opening on assumed ventral side (no anus).
evidence: This is part of the emended diagnosis based on morphological observations.

claim: Only two forms, Saccorhytus and Beretella, are currently placed within Saccorhytida.
source: Only two forms, Saccorhytus and Beretella are currently placed within Saccorhytida, making it premature to formally define intermediate taxonomic categories such as an order and a family.
evidence: This is a statement about the current taxonomic composition of Saccorhytida.

claim: The body of Beretella spinosa is secondarily phosphatized.
source: The body of Beretella spinosa is secondarily phosphatized and has a consistent beret-like three-dimensional shape in the lateral view.
evidence: This is a taphonomic observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Beretella spinosa has a consistent beret-like three-dimensional shape in the lateral view.
source: The body of Beretella spinosa is secondarily phosphatized and has a consistent beret-like three-dimensional shape in the lateral view.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The length, width, and height of Beretella spinosa range from 1000–2900 µm, 975–2450 µm, and 500–1000 µm, respectively.
source: Its length, width, and height range from 1000–2900 µm, 975–2450 µm, and 500–1000 µm, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-I, Supplementary file 1a-c).
evidence: These are measurements taken from the fossil specimens.

claim: The ratio of the maximal length to width of Beretella spinosa is 1.6:1.
source: The ratio of the maximal length to width is 1.6:1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This is a calculated ratio from measurements of the fossil specimens.

claim: Beretella spinosa shows a small lateral constriction at approximately mid-length.
source: As seen in top view, B. spinosa shows a small lateral constriction at approximately mid-length (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The body of Beretella spinosa has a convex, assumedly dorsal side with one, presumably posterior end more elevated than the other.
source: The body has a convex, assumedly dorsal side with one, presumably posterior end more elevated than the other (Figure 1B, E, I and K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I).
evidence: This is a morphological observation with interpretation of body orientation.

claim: The opposite, assumedly ventral side of Beretella spinosa is less well preserved and seems to have been originally flattened.
source: The opposite, assumedly ventral side is less well preserved and seems to have been originally flattened.
evidence: This is a morphological observation with interpretation of body orientation.

claim: The convex side of Beretella spinosa bears a complex ornamented pattern made of five sets (S1‒S5) of spiny sclerites directed towards the more elevated end.
source: The convex side bears a complex ornamented pattern made of five sets (S1‒S5) of spiny sclerites directed towards the more elevated end (Figures 1A, B, D, E, H‒K, 2A, B, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The sclerites of Beretella spinosa were originally pointed.
source: These sclerites were originally pointed (Figure 1A, B, D, E, H-K and Figure 2B, K, L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, G), but most of them were broken thus revealing an internal cavity and an ellipsoidal transverse section (Figures 1A, B, H‒K, 2A-E, G).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Most sclerites of Beretella spinosa were broken, revealing an internal cavity and an ellipsoidal transverse section.
source: These sclerites were originally pointed (Figure 1A, B, D, E, H-K and Figure 2B, K, L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, G), but most of them were broken thus revealing an internal cavity and an ellipsoidal transverse section (Figures 1A, B, H‒K, 2A-E, G).
evidence: This is a taphonomic observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The broken sclerites of Beretella spinosa show an inner and outer phosphatic layer (thickness ca. 20–50 µm) often separated by a thin empty space.
source: The broken sclerites show an inner and outer phosphatic layer (thickness ca. 20–50 µm) often separated by a thin empty space (Figure 2G-L).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The convex side of Beretella spinosa bears six prominent conical sclerites (S3) all with a rounded to elliptical well-delimited broad base.
source: The convex side bears six prominent conical sclerites (S3) all with a rounded to elliptical well-delimited broad base, distributed in two longitudinal symmetrical pairs with two additional sclerites at both ends of the sagittal plane (Figures 1 and 2D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-I).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The S3 sclerites of Beretella spinosa are distributed in two longitudinal symmetrical pairs with two additional sclerites at both ends of the sagittal plane.
source: The convex side bears six prominent conical sclerites (S3) all with a rounded to elliptical well-delimited broad base, distributed in two longitudinal symmetrical pairs with two additional sclerites at both ends of the sagittal plane (Figures 1 and 2D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-I).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: A low-relief stripe runs in a sagittal position on Beretella spinosa and vanishes towards the elevated end.
source: A low-relief stripe runs in a sagittal position and vanishes towards the elevated end.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The sagittal stripe of Beretella spinosa is topped by a row of aligned spines (S1).
source: It is topped by a row of aligned spines (S1, Figure 1A); the one closer to the more elevated end being more tubular and longer.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The S1 spine closer to the more elevated end of Beretella spinosa is more tubular and longer.
source: It is topped by a row of aligned spines (S1, Figure 1A); the one closer to the more elevated end being more tubular and longer.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The S1 row of Beretella spinosa is flanked on both sides by smaller aligned spines (S2).
source: This row is flanked on both sides by smaller aligned spines (S2, Figures 1A, D, H ,, 2A‒C).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Two relatively sinuous rows of six tiny spines (S4 and S5) are present parallel to the lateral margins of Beretella spinosa.
source: Two relatively sinuous rows of six tiny spines are present parallel to the lateral margins (S4 and S5, Figures 1B, E, H‒J, 2D, E).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The convex side of Beretella spinosa bears a polygonal micro-ornament (mesh size ca. 5 µm wide).
source: The convex side bears a polygonal micro-ornament (mesh size ca. 5 µm wide, Figure 2F, Supplementary file 1a-c).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Clusters of spherical phosphatized grains (diameter ca. 20 µm) occur near the sclerite base of Beretella spinosa.
source: Clusters of spherical phosphatized grains (diameter ca. 20 µm) occur near the sclerite base (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a taphonomic observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: In most specimens of Beretella spinosa, the flattened side is occupied by a relatively large opening (1200 and 600 µm in maximal length and width, respectively) with irregularly defined margins.
source: In most specimens, the flattened side is occupied by a relatively large opening (1200 and 600 µm in maximal length and width, respectively) with irregularly defined margins (Figure 1C and F, see also Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The flattened side of Beretella spinosa is often largely missing and opens into a spacious internal cavity with no signs of internal organs.
source: The flattened side is often largely missing and opens into a spacious internal cavity with no signs of internal organs (e.g. gut and pharynx; Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This is a taphonomic and morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: One specimen of Beretella spinosa shows a tiny spine on the margin of the flattened side.
source: One specimen shows a tiny spine on the margin of the flattened side (Figure 1F and G), which differs from other spiny sclerites (S1-S5).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from a specific fossil specimen.

claim: The length of studied specimens of Beretella spinosa ranges from 1.0 to 2.9 mm.
source: The length of studied specimens ranges from 1.0 to 2.9 mm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: These are measurements from the fossil specimens.

claim: Whether growth of Beretella spinosa was continuous or took place via successive moulting stages could not be tested due to the small number of specimens available for measurements.
source: Whether growth was continuous or instead took place via successive moulting stages and cuticular renewal (ecdysis) could not be tested due to the small number of specimens (N=17) available for measurements.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: No major morphological variations can be seen between the smallest and largest specimens of Beretella spinosa.
source: No major morphological variations (e.g. a sclerite pattern) can be seen between the smallest and largest specimens of B. spinosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This is a comparative observation across specimens.

claim: In the vast majority of extinct and extant invertebrates for which antero-posterior polarity is defined, sclerites point backwards.
source: In the vast majority of extinct and extant invertebrates for which antero-posterior polarity is defined on the basis of independent criteria (e.g. position of the mouth), sclerites point backwards (e.g. Cambrian scalidophoran worms [Han et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2004] and Wiwaxia [Zhang et al., 2015a]).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to other fossil taxa.

claim: Sclerites of Beretella spinosa most probably point backwards.
source: This is most probably also the case with Beretella (Figure 1A, D and J).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other invertebrates.

claim: Protective sclerites such as spines most commonly occur on the dorsal side of bilaterians.
source: The dorsoventral polarity of Beretella is supported by the fact that protective sclerites such as spines most commonly occur on the dorsal side of bilaterians (Figure 1A, D and J).
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge of bilaterian anatomy.

claim: Beretella spinosa has no exact equivalent in any Cambrian animals except Saccorhytus coronarius.
source: Beretella spinosa has no exact equivalent in any Cambrian animals except Saccorhytus coronarius, an enigmatic, sac-like ecdysozoan (Han et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022; Shu and Han, 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Both Beretella and Saccorhytus share a tiny, poorly differentiated ellipsoidal body, and a set of prominent bilaterally arranged spiny sclerites.
source: Both forms share a tiny, poorly differentiated ellipsoidal body, and a set of prominent bilaterally arranged spiny sclerites.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: The broad-based conical sclerites (S3) of Beretella are almost identical to those of Saccorhytus.
source: Indeed, the broad-based conical sclerites (S3) of Beretella are almost identical to those of Saccorhytus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and have counterparts among scalidophoran worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: The S3 sclerites of Beretella have counterparts among scalidophoran worms.
source: Indeed, the broad-based conical sclerites (S3) of Beretella are almost identical to those of Saccorhytus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and have counterparts among scalidophoran worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: Beretella and Saccorhytus differ in number, ornamented structures, shape, and spatial arrangement.
source: However, they differ in number, ornamented structures, shape, and spatial arrangement (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: Beretella has a much more pronounced dorsoventral differentiation than Saccorhytus.
source: Beretella has a much more pronounced dorsoventral differentiation than Saccorhytus and its cuticle seems to have been harder and less flexible (see details in Supplementary file 1a-c), which altogether the hypothesis of Saccorhytus being the larval stage of Beretella unlikely.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: The cuticle of Beretella seems to have been harder and less flexible than that of Saccorhytus.
source: Beretella has a much more pronounced dorsoventral differentiation than Saccorhytus and its cuticle seems to have been harder and less flexible (see details in Supplementary file 1a-c), which altogether the hypothesis of Saccorhytus being the larval stage of Beretella unlikely.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: The hypothesis of Saccorhytus being the larval stage of Beretella is unlikely.
source: Beretella has a much more pronounced dorsoventral differentiation than Saccorhytus and its cuticle seems to have been harder and less flexible (see details in Supplementary file 1a-c), which altogether the hypothesis of Saccorhytus being the larval stage of Beretella unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological differences.

claim: Both Beretella and Saccorhytus differ from other known ecdysozoans in the lack of an elongated body, introvert, annulations, and through gut.
source: Both Beretella and Saccorhytus differ from other known ecdysozoans in the lack of an elongated body, introvert, annulations, and through gut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1a-c).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation.

claim: All bilaterian animals have a digestive system with at least one opening that corresponds to the mouth.
source: All bilaterian animals have a digestive system with at least one opening that corresponds to the mouth (Brusca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a general statement about bilaterian anatomy supported by citation.

claim: The mouth of Beretella is likely to be found ventrally.
source: Although the presumed oral area of Beretella is poorly preserved (ventral side often pushed in and largely destroyed), its mouth is likely to be found ventrally (see description), since no other opening occurs on its dorsal side, except those created by broken sclerites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of other openings on the dorsal side.

claim: No other opening occurs on the dorsal side of Beretella, except those created by broken sclerites.
source: Although the presumed oral area of Beretella is poorly preserved (ventral side often pushed in and largely destroyed), its mouth is likely to be found ventrally (see description), since no other opening occurs on its dorsal side, except those created by broken sclerites.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: The well-defined dorsoventral polarity of Beretella suggests that the animal was resting on its ventral (flattened) side.
source: The well-defined dorsoventral polarity of Beretella would suggest that the animal was resting on its ventral (flattened) side, the spiny dorsal side playing a protective role.
evidence: This is an inference about the life orientation of the animal.

claim: The spiny dorsal side of Beretella played a protective role.
source: The well-defined dorsoventral polarity of Beretella would suggest that the animal was resting on its ventral (flattened) side, the spiny dorsal side playing a protective role.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of the spiny sclerites.

claim: The scleritome of Beretella consists of isolated conical sclerites that were the cuticular outgrowths of a seemingly rigid integument.
source: Its scleritome consists of isolated conical sclerites that were the cuticular outgrowths of a seemingly rigid integument that covered both sides of the animal.
evidence: This is a morphological observation and interpretation.

claim: The conical sclerites of Beretella have close counterparts in Cambrian ecdysozoans such as scalidophoran worms, lobopodians, and Saccorhytus.
source: Such conical sclerites have close counterparts in Cambrian ecdysozoans such as scalidophoran worms (e.g. Eokinorhynchus Zhang et al., 2015b), lobopodians (e.g. Onychodictyon ferox Hou et al., 1991) and even more clearly Saccorhytus that recent cladistic analyses resolved as a branch of the total-group Ecdysozoa (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Recent cladistic analyses resolved Saccorhytus as a branch of the total-group Ecdysozoa.
source: Such conical sclerites have close counterparts in Cambrian ecdysozoans such as scalidophoran worms (e.g. Eokinorhynchus Zhang et al., 2015b), lobopodians (e.g. Onychodictyon ferox Hou et al., 1991) and even more clearly Saccorhytus that recent cladistic analyses resolved as a branch of the total-group Ecdysozoa (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: The conical sclerites of Beretella and Saccorhytus are unknown in other animal groups.
source: These sclerites, unknown in other animal groups, suggest that both Saccorhytus and Beretella belongs to Ecdysozoa (moulting animals), although more direct fossil evidence such as exuviae or features suggesting cuticular moulting (Daley and Drage, 2016; Wang et al., 2019) has yet to be found.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of animal morphology.

claim: The conical sclerites suggest that both Saccorhytus and Beretella belong to Ecdysozoa.
source: These sclerites, unknown in other animal groups, suggest that both Saccorhytus and Beretella belongs to Ecdysozoa (moulting animals), although more direct fossil evidence such as exuviae or features suggesting cuticular moulting (Daley and Drage, 2016; Wang et al., 2019) has yet to be found.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological comparison and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Direct fossil evidence such as exuviae or features suggesting cuticular moulting in Beretella and Saccorhytus has yet to be found.
source: These sclerites, unknown in other animal groups, suggest that both Saccorhytus and Beretella belongs to Ecdysozoa (moulting animals), although more direct fossil evidence such as exuviae or features suggesting cuticular moulting (Daley and Drage, 2016; Wang et al., 2019) has yet to be found.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of certain types of fossil evidence.

claim: Both Beretella and Saccorhytus join in a clade (Saccorhytida) and are resolved as members of total-group Ecdysozoa.
source: Both taxa join in a clade (Saccorhytida, Figure 3A‒C) and are resolved as members of total-group Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analyses performed in the study.

claim: Saccorhytida is the sister group of Cycloneuralia plus Panarthropoda (crown-group Ecdysozoa).
source: This clade is the sister group of Cycloneuralia plus Panarthropoda (crown-group Ecdysozoa, Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4, Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analyses performed in the study.

claim: The body plan of Saccorhytida is markedly different from that of crown-group ecdysozoans.
source: These results are consistent with the body plan of Saccorhytida being markedly different from that of crown-group ecdysozoans that all have an elongated body and differentiated structures, such as, in Cycloneuralia, the introvert and pharyngeal complex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological statement.

claim: Crown-group ecdysozoans all have an elongated body and differentiated structures.
source: These results are consistent with the body plan of Saccorhytida being markedly different from that of crown-group ecdysozoans that all have an elongated body and differentiated structures, such as, in Cycloneuralia, the introvert and pharyngeal complex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological statement.

claim: Cycloneuralia have an introvert and pharyngeal complex.
source: These results are consistent with the body plan of Saccorhytida being markedly different from that of crown-group ecdysozoans that all have an elongated body and differentiated structures, such as, in Cycloneuralia, the introvert and pharyngeal complex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of Cycloneuralia.

claim: Molecular clock analyses often place the divergence of Ecdysozoa relatively deep into the Ediacaran.
source: Molecular clock analyses often place the divergence of Ecdysozoa relatively deep into the Ediacaran (Howard et al., 2022; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013), thus highlighting major discrepancy with the known fossil record of the group.
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular clock studies.

claim: There is major discrepancy between molecular clock estimates and the known fossil record of Ecdysozoa.
source: Molecular clock analyses often place the divergence of Ecdysozoa relatively deep into the Ediacaran (Howard et al., 2022; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013), thus highlighting major discrepancy with the known fossil record of the group.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of molecular and fossil data.

claim: Potential ecdysozoans occur in the late Precambrian as suggested by sclerites resembling scalids of priapulids found in Ediacaran Small Carbonaceous Fossils assemblages.
source: Potential ecdysozoans occur in the late Precambrian as suggested by sclerites resembling scalids of priapulids, found in Ediacaran Small Carbonaceous Fossils assemblages (Moczydłowska et al., 2015) and locomotion traces presumably made by scalidophoran worms (Buatois et al., 2014; Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fossil evidence.

claim: Locomotion traces presumably made by scalidophoran worms occur in the late Precambrian.
source: Potential ecdysozoans occur in the late Precambrian as suggested by sclerites resembling scalids of priapulids, found in Ediacaran Small Carbonaceous Fossils assemblages (Moczydłowska et al., 2015) and locomotion traces presumably made by scalidophoran worms (Buatois et al., 2014; Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to trace fossil evidence.

claim: Scalidophorans are potentially the oldest known representatives of Ecdysozoa.
source: In the absence of fossil data for other groups such as nematoids, scalidophorans are potentially the oldest known representatives of Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record.

claim: Recent Bayesian analyses recover Scalidophora as the sister-group to Nematoida + Panarthropoda.
source: Recent Bayesian analyses based on a large molecular data set obtained from the 8 extant ecdysozoan phyla recover Scalidophora as the sister-group to Nematoida +Panarthropoda and suggest that ecdysozoans probably diverged in the Ediacaran, possibly some 23 million years before the oldest fossil occurrence (trace fossils) of the group (Howard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a molecular phylogenetic study.

claim: Ecdysozoans probably diverged in the Ediacaran, possibly some 23 million years before the oldest fossil occurrence of the group.
source: Recent Bayesian analyses based on a large molecular data set obtained from the 8 extant ecdysozoan phyla recover Scalidophora as the sister-group to Nematoida +Panarthropoda and suggest that ecdysozoans probably diverged in the Ediacaran, possibly some 23 million years before the oldest fossil occurrence (trace fossils) of the group (Howard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a molecular phylogenetic study.

claim: Howard et al. (2020) drew conclusions based on Acosmia, an assumed stem-ecdysozoan worm from early Cambrian Chengjiang Lagerstätte.
source: Although this study does not speculate on the nature of the last common ancestor of Ecdysozoa, it is consistent with the view that the earliest representatives of the group were probably worm-like, relatively elongated animals. (Howard et al., 2020) drew comparable conclusions based on Acosmia, an assumed stem-ecdysozoan worm from early Cambrian Chengjiang Lagerstätte.
evidence: This is a statement about another study's conclusions.

claim: The re-evaluation of Acosmia suggests a less basal position either within the total-group Cycloneuralia or among crown-group Ecdysozoa.
source: However, the re-evaluation of the morphological characteristics of this worm rather suggests a less basal position either within the total-group Cycloneuralia (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) or among crown-group Ecdysozoa (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analyses performed in the study.

claim: The ellipsoidal (non-vermiform) shape of saccorhytids and their position as the sister group of the crown-group Ecdysozoa reopens the debate on the nature of the ancestral ecdysozoan.
source: The ellipsoidal (non-vermiform) shape of saccorhytids and their position as the sister group of the crown-group Ecdysozoa clearly reopens the debate on the nature of the ancestral ecdysozoan (Figure 4) and has led to explore alternative evolutionary hypotheses, in particular: (i) does the enigmatic saccorhytid body plan results from anatomical simplification? (ii) to what extent may these animals shed light on the nature of the earliest ecdysozoans?
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: A relatively simple body plan and tiny size is often seen as resulting from anatomical simplification and miniaturization.
source: A relatively simple body plan and tiny size is often seen as resulting from anatomical simplification (e.g. reduction of digestive system) and miniaturization (micrometric size) in possible relation with the adaptation to specialized ecological niches or parasitism (Hanken and Wake, 1993).
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary processes supported by citation.

claim: Some extant scalidophoran worms living in interstitial habitats such as loriciferans have a miniaturized body compared with their macroscopic counterparts.
source: For example, some extant scalidophoran worms living in interstitial (meiobenthic) habitats such as loriciferans have a miniaturized body (Kristensen, 1983) compared with their macroscopic counterparts (e.g. Priapulus Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on loriciferans.

claim: Miniaturized loriciferans retain a through gut and a functional introvert and show no sign of drastic internal simplification.
source: However, they retain a through gut and a functional introvert and show no sign of drastic internal simplification (Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on scalidophoran anatomy.

claim: Anatomical reduction is a typical feature of parasitism.
source: Anatomical reduction is a typical feature of parasitism (Hanken and Wake, 1993) that is well-represented among extant ecdysozoans such as nematodes (Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2013c).
evidence: This is a general statement about parasitism supported by citation.

claim: Nematodes underwent no simplification of their digestive system despite being relatively small.
source: Although relatively small (ca. 0.1–2.5 mm long), nematodes underwent no simplification of their digestive system.
evidence: This is a statement about nematode anatomy.

claim: Saccorhytids have no specialized features that would point to any adaptation to ecto- or endo-parasitic lifestyles.
source: Saccorhytids have no specialized features (e.g. anchoring or piercing structures) that would point to any adaptation to ecto- or endo-parasitic lifestyles (Cong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by citation.

claim: Saccorhytus has been interpreted as a possible interstitial animal based on its micrometric size.
source: Saccorhytus has been interpreted (Han et al., 2017) as a possible interstitial animal based on its micrometric size which corresponds to that of the extant meiofauna.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Simplification of saccorhytids from an elongated animal would involve considerable anatomical transformations such as the loss of tubular organization, introvert and pharynx in addition to that of the digestive system.
source: If we accept the hypothesis that saccorhytids result from simplification, then we need to determine its origin. Simplification of saccorhytids from an elongated animal (e.g. cycloneuralian worm with a through gut and terminal mouth) is difficult to conceive because it would involve considerable anatomical transformations such as the loss of tubular organization, introvert and pharynx in addition to that of the digestive system (Figure 4, and Supplementary file 1d, e).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the difficulty of a particular evolutionary scenario.

claim: Saccorhytids are seen as an early off-shot from the stem-line Ecdysozoa that possibly retained important features of the body plan of ancestral ecdysozoans.
source: We propose here an alternative evolutionary hypothesis (Figure 4) in which saccorhytids are replaced within the broader framework of the origin and early diversification of moulting animals. Saccorhytids are seen as an early off-shot from the stem-line Ecdysozoa (see cladistic analysis above) that possibly retained important features of the body plan of ancestral ecdysozoans.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Cuticular secretion and the loss of cilia would be the first of a series of evolutionary events that led to the rise of Ecdysozoa.
source: The cuticular secretion and the loss of cilia (Valentine and Collins, 2000) would be the first of a series of evolutionary events (Figure 4) that led to the rise of Ecdysozoa.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about early ecdysozoan evolution supported by citation.

claim: Moulting reconciled body growth and cuticular protection.
source: Moulting (shedding of the old cuticle via apolysis and its renewal) reconciled body growth and cuticular protection (Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2007).
evidence: This is a functional statement about moulting supported by citation.

claim: Cuticle secretion and moulting may have been quasi-simultaneous innovations that took place over a relatively short time interval.
source: Cuticle secretion and moulting may have been quasi-simultaneous innovations that took place over a relatively short time interval.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the timing of evolutionary innovations.

claim: The very first ecdysozoans are tentatively represented as small epibenthic or interstitial slow-moving non-elongated animals from which saccorhytids may have evolved.
source: The nature of the very first ecdysozoans is hypothetical and lacks fossil evidence. However, they are tentatively represented here as small epibenthic or interstitial slow-moving non- elongated animals from which saccorhytids may have evolved.
evidence: This is a speculative reconstruction of ancestral ecdysozoans.

claim: The ancestral ecdysozoan stock would have given rise to elongated and tubular ecdysozoans through stepwise anatomical transformations.
source: In our scenario, this ancestral ecdysozoan stock would have also given rise to elongated and tubular ecdysozoans through stepwise anatomical transformations such as the body elongation, the differentiation of key morpho-functional structures such as the pharynx and the introvert and the shift of the ventral mouth to a terminal position (Martín-Durán and Hejnol, 2015; Figure 4, Supplementary file 1d, e).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario proposed by the authors.

claim: The mouth shift from ventral to terminal arising in crown ecdysozoans is consistent with the chronology of divergence of animal lineages and the fact that the mouth of most spiralians is ventral.
source: This mouth shift from ventral to terminal arising in crown ecdysozoans is consistent with the chronology of divergence of animal lineages and the fact that the mouth of most spiralians is ventral (Martín-Durán and Hejnol, 2015; Nielsen, 2019; Ortega-Hernández et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mouth position evolution.

claim: Developmental studies show that embryos of extant cycloneuralians have a ventral mouth that moves to a terminal position towards the adult stage.
source: Developmental studies show that embryos of extant cycloneuralians have a ventral mouth that moves to a terminal position towards the adult stage (Martín-Durán and Hejnol, 2015; Nielsen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: Important changes in the functioning of marine ecosystems occurred in the early Cambrian such as interactive relationships between animal species, exemplified by predation.
source: Important changes in the functioning of marine ecosystems occurred in the early Cambrian such as interactive relationships between animal species, exemplified by predation (Vannier and Chen, 2005; Vermeij, 1977) and may have acted as drivers in the evolution of early ecdysozoans, in promoting burrowing into sediment and the colonization of endobenthic habitats for the first time (Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Cambrian ecology.

claim: Ecological changes in the early Cambrian may have acted as drivers in the evolution of early ecdysozoans, promoting burrowing into sediment and the colonization of endobenthic habitats.
source: Important changes in the functioning of marine ecosystems occurred in the early Cambrian such as interactive relationships between animal species, exemplified by predation (Vannier and Chen, 2005; Vermeij, 1977) and may have acted as drivers in the evolution of early ecdysozoans, in promoting burrowing into sediment and the colonization of endobenthic habitats for the first time (Vannier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary drivers supported by citations.

claim: Burrowing into the sediment could be seen as the evolutionary response of epibenthic animals such as ancestral ecdysozoans to escape visual predation.
source: Burrowing into the sediment could be seen as the evolutionary response of epibenthic animals such as ancestral ecdysozoans to escape visual predation (Daley et al., 2013; Vannier and Chen, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary responses supported by citations.

claim: The migration to endobenthic shelters was made possible by the development of a resistant cuticular layer that strongly reduced physical damage caused by friction with the sediment and provided anchoring points.
source: We hypothesize that this migration to endobenthic shelters was made possible by the development of a resistant cuticular layer (Figure 4) that strongly reduced physical damage caused by friction with the sediment and provided anchoring points (e.g. scalids and sclerites).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of the cuticle in burrowing.

claim: Saccorhytids became rapidly extinct during the Cambrian.
source: Whereas saccorhytids became rapidly extinct during the Cambrian, worms massively colonized endobenthic habitats, resulting in bioturbation and ecological turnover.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record.

claim: Worms massively colonized endobenthic habitats during the Cambrian, resulting in bioturbation and ecological turnover.
source: Whereas saccorhytids became rapidly extinct during the Cambrian, worms massively colonized endobenthic habitats, resulting in bioturbation and ecological turnover.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of the Cambrian fossil record.

claim: Fourteen specimens of Beretella spinosa were recovered from Member 5 of the Yanjiahe Formation.
source: Fourteen specimens of Beretella spinosa were recovered from samples (siliceous-phosphatic, intraclastic limestone) collected from Member 5 of the Yanjiahe Formation, Yanjiahe section near Yichang City, Hubei Province, China (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the material studied.

claim: Specimens of Beretella spinosa were obtained by digesting rocks in 10% acetic acid.
source: These were obtained by digesting the rocks in 10% acetic acid.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: Faunal elements associated with Beretella spinosa in residues are mainly tiny molluscs.
source: Faunal elements associated with Beretella spinosa in residues are mainly tiny molluscs (CUBar21-4 and CUBar206-6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation about the associated fauna.
